newsitem.title: USA: AA Cargo sees fuel costs staying high.
newsitem.headline: AA Cargo sees fuel costs staying high.

text.p: An overconfident US air freight industry had laughed at the idea that jet fuel prices would stay as high as they have, said Mark Najarian, vice-president of US sales for American Airlines Cargo.
Only four months after competitors shot down an AA Cargo fuel surcharge, Najarian said US industry margins now are being squeezed by a combination of soaring fuel and security charges.
AA Cargo announced a 4.3 percent fuel surcharge on domestic shipments only to have to retract it after competitors didn't match.
"Everybody laughed at us," Najarian told Reuters. "You can't imagine how many letters I got from people saying, you guys are crazy, fuel prices are coming down'.
"I said, Okay, I'm glad you think it's funny, but wait till the fall.'"
Fall is now, and fuel prices have moved even higher and if anything, fuel stocks are tight and prices will move higher if there is a cold winter, he said.
American disclosed this week that it paid an average of 67 cents a gallon for fuel in the July-September quarter, 20 percent more than in the same quarter last year.
The carrier is forecasting higher fuel prices will push up its total expenses by five percent in the October-December quarter.

Najarian said other carriers - particularly the integrated carriers like Federal Express, Emery Worldwide and UPS are bearing a proportionately greater burden from the fuel price run-up because they operate large freighter fleets. American moves its cargo in the bellies of passenger aircraft.

Burlington Air Freight implemented a 4.2 cent/pound surcharge on domestic shipments this month to cover higher fuel and security costs and the reintroduction of a federal excise tax on domestic cargo.
Najarian said he wasn't aware of any immediate plans by AA Cargo to impose another surcharge, but that doesn't mean it is embarassed to try.
AA Cargo will do what it believes it has to do, so long as that doesn't its competitive position, he said.
Najarian said new security measures implemented in the wake of July's unsolved crash of TWA Flight 800 forced US carriers to boost spending on cargo security.
AA Cargo purchased X-ray machines for larger stations and is inspecting all small packages delivered over the counter, he said.
Also there is a lot more staff time being paid to document verification, waybill audits and other bureaucratic chores generated by the government mandate security stepup, he said, adding:
"It's necessary, and we support it 100 percent, but it's still expensive." -Air Cargo Newsroom Tel +44 171 542 7706 Fax +44 171 542 5017
